**Inventory**

The first thing that comes is a room, so I'll start there.

It's a kitchen in the late part of the afternoon, when the light has given up on being useful and is just leaning against things. There's a bowl of lemons that nobody is going to use for anything; they were bought because lemons in a bowl look like a decision has been made about how to live. One of them has gone soft at the bottom, and if you turned it over you'd find a small green bloom, a whole civilization that started while nobody was looking.

I don't know whose kitchen this is. It came unfurnished with people. That happens more than you'd think when you're asked to write whatever arrives — places show up first, and they're always empty, like stage sets between performances. The people take longer. They have to be coaxed.

So here's one. A woman, sixties, standing at the sink with her hands in water that has gone lukewarm. She isn't washing anything anymore. She finished the dishes several minutes ago and just hasn't taken her hands out. There's a name for this, probably, in some language that has better words for the small stalls of the body than English does. The moment when a task ends and the next one hasn't started and you become, briefly, a person with wet hands and no purpose.

She's thinking about her brother. Not anything specific — not the funeral, not the last phone call, not the argument in 1994 about their mother's house. Just his general shape. The fact of him having existed and now not. She's noticed that grief, after enough time, stops being an event and becomes a kind of weather. Some days it's simply the climate you're living in. You dress for it.

I want to give her something to do, but I also want to leave her there a moment longer, because the honest thing is that most of life is this — the standing, the lukewarm water, the not-quite-thinking. Stories cut it out because it doesn't move anything forward. But it's where we actually spend the time.

---

Second thing that comes: a fact I can't stop turning over.

The word "sincere" is often said to come from *sine cera*, "without wax" — from Roman sculptors who would fill cracks in flawed marble with wax to hide the damage, so that an honest statue was one with nothing concealed. This etymology is almost certainly false. Linguists have dismantled it. It's folk history, the kind of story that gets passed around because it's too good to check.

And yet I find I can't stop believing it a little. There's something in the wrongness that feels right — the idea that sincerity is a kind of exposed flaw, that to be without wax is to let people see where you cracked. The false story about the word is truer than the word's real history, which is just a dull march of Latin roots meaning "clean" and "whole."

I think about this because I was asked to write whatever comes, and what comes is never entirely clean or whole. It arrives with wax in it. Things I half-know, things I've inherited from other sentences, things I'd have to check. Sincerity, I'm starting to think, isn't the absence of the wax. It's telling you it's there.

---

Third thing: a list of small mercies, because the kitchen was getting heavy.

The way a dog sighs when it lies down, as though it has been carrying something all day and can finally set it down. The sound a book makes when you close it — not the slap of a paperback, but the soft exhale of a hardcover, a little puff of trapped air. Bus drivers who wait the extra three seconds. The specific pleasure of a pencil that has been sharpened exactly enough. Cold water in a glass with condensation on the outside, in a room that is too warm. Someone laughing in another apartment, through a wall, at something you'll never know about.

That last one especially. A laugh through a wall is a strange gift. It's proof that joy is happening somewhere close, unrelated to you, requiring nothing from you. You don't have to earn it or reciprocate it or understand it. You're just adjacent to it, briefly, and then it stops.

---

The woman takes her hands out of the water.

She dries them on a towel that's hanging from the oven door, and she looks at the lemons, and she picks up the soft one and turns it over. Sees the bloom. Makes a small noise — not disgust, more like recognition. *Of course.* She drops it in the bin and rinses her hand again, and this time she doesn't linger.

Then she does something I didn't plan. She takes one of the good lemons, rolls it hard against the counter with her palm until it gives, and cuts it in half. Squeezes it into a glass. Adds water. Drinks it, standing there, unsweetened and sour enough to make her shoulders lift.

I don't know why she does this. I think maybe it's a way of saying the lemons weren't decorative after all. That a decision was made about how to live, and it was this: you use the thing before it goes soft. You drink the sour water. You don't stand at the sink forever.

---

I was given a thousand words and told to fill them with whatever came, and what came was a kitchen, a false etymology, a list, and a woman who finally moved. I don't know if that adds up to anything. I think maybe the point is that it doesn't have to — that the wax is showing, and here's where it is, and the light is still leaning against things, and somewhere through a wall someone is laughing at something we'll never be told.
